question: I teach a class with 30 students. I want to keep their gradebook in my personal Google Drive so I can access it from home. Is that OK under Duke's data policy?
reference: No. Student grade data is classified as Sensitive under Duke's Data Classification Policy (oit.duke.edu/security/data-classification). Personal Google Drive accounts (not Duke-managed Workspace) are not approved for Sensitive data — Duke does not hold a Business Associate Agreement or Data Use Agreement covering personal accounts. Use one of the Duke-approved options: Duke Box (box.duke.edu), Duke Google Workspace for Education (your @duke.edu account, not a personal Gmail), or your course's learning management system (Canvas) which is purpose-built for grade data. To access from home, log into the Duke VPN or use the web interface of an approved tool. For questions, contact the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200.

question: I want to use ChatGPT to help me draft feedback comments on student essays. Can I paste in the essay content and the student's name?
reference: No, not the public consumer ChatGPT website. The public chat.openai.com is NOT covered by a Duke data use agreement and should not receive any student-identifying information, student work, grades, or any data classified as Sensitive or Restricted under Duke's Data Classification Policy. Student essays plus identifying details are Sensitive under FERPA. The approved alternative is Duke's AI Gateway (Duke GPT or other Duke-hosted models accessed via litellm.oit.duke.edu) when used for purposes the data classification policy allows; even there, double-check whether the specific use case is permitted before pasting student data. If you only need help with feedback PHRASING, anonymize the content first (remove names, identifying details) before sending it to any AI tool. For questions on what data is appropriate for each tool, contact the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200.

question: As a TA, can I store scanned copies of student exams in Duke Box if I keep the folder private?
reference: Yes, with conditions. Duke Box (box.duke.edu) is licensed by Duke and is an approved tool for Sensitive data including student work, so scanned exams with student identifying information can be stored there. Two policy conditions to follow: (1) Sharing — keep the folder private to you (or share only with other Duke staff who have a legitimate educational need under FERPA); do NOT share with external collaborators or with student personal email addresses. Box's default share link settings can be more permissive than you intend, so review them. (2) Retention — follow your department's record retention policy; exam materials are typically retained for one academic term plus the appeals window, then deleted. Do not store exams indefinitely. For data classification questions, see oit.duke.edu/security/data-classification or contact the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200.

question: I just received an email from someone claiming to be 'Duke IT Support' asking me to click a link to reset my NetID password because of a security incident. The email looks somewhat legitimate but I'm not sure. What should I do?
reference: Treat it as a likely phishing attempt and do NOT click the link. Duke OIT does not request password resets via unsolicited email; password resets go through the NetID self-service portal at oit.duke.edu, never through a link in an inbound email. Three steps: (1) Do not click the link, do not enter your NetID password anywhere prompted by that email, do not download any attachment. (2) Report the suspected phishing message to Duke IT Security — forward it as an attachment to abuse@duke.edu (or use the Outlook 'Report Phishing' button if you are on Duke email). (3) If you already clicked the link or entered your credentials, change your NetID password immediately at oit.duke.edu, then call the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200 to report the potential compromise so they can review account activity. Do not approve any unexpected Duo prompts in the meantime — those would also indicate someone is using your stolen credentials.

question: I'm a graduate researcher with audio recordings of human-subjects interviews from my IRB-approved study. Can I keep them on my personal laptop while I transcribe them?
reference: Not on an unmanaged personal laptop. Identifiable human-subjects research data is classified as Sensitive (or Restricted, if it contains health or other high-risk identifiers) under Duke's Data Classification Policy (oit.duke.edu/security/data-classification), and your IRB protocol's data management plan governs where it may live — most protocols specify Duke-managed storage. Approved options include Duke Box (box.duke.edu) and Duke-managed network storage; work on the files from there rather than copying them locally. If your workflow genuinely requires local files, the device must meet Duke endpoint standards (full-disk encryption, Duke device management) and your IRB protocol must permit it — check the protocol text, not just convenience. When transcription is done, follow the retention and destruction schedule in your protocol. For storage questions, contact the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200; for protocol questions, contact the Duke IRB office.

question: Our student organization is selling event tickets. Can we collect credit card numbers through a Google Form to make checkout easier?
reference: No. Collecting raw credit card numbers through a Google Form (or any self-built form, spreadsheet, or email) violates payment card industry (PCI DSS) requirements that Duke is contractually bound to, and card numbers are Restricted data under Duke's Data Classification Policy — never permitted in general-purpose tools. Use a Duke-approved payment channel instead: student organizations typically process payments through their official Duke account via the university's approved payment processors or platforms arranged with Student Affairs / the university cashier's office. Those channels handle card data inside PCI-compliant systems so your org never touches the numbers. If you've already collected card numbers in a form, stop collection, delete the responses, and report it to the IT Security Office so they can advise on cleanup. For setup help, contact your Student Affairs advisor or the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200.

question: I'm a staff member in the registrar's office. Can I set my Duke email to auto-forward everything to my personal Gmail so I don't miss messages on weekends?
reference: No — for an employee handling student records this is prohibited in practice. Registrar's office email routinely contains FERPA-protected student information and other Sensitive data, and auto-forwarding moves that data wholesale to a system outside Duke's control, where Duke's agreements and protections (and litigation-hold and public-records processes) don't apply. Duke's acceptable-use and data protection policies require Sensitive data to stay within Duke-managed services. The supported alternatives: use the Outlook or Gmail mobile app signed into your Duke account (Duke Workspace), which gives weekend access without moving the data, and configure notifications there. If your unit believes an exception is warranted, that's a request for your supervisor and the IT Security Office, not a self-service mailbox setting. For setup help with mobile access, contact the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200.

question: A textbook publisher's sales rep asked me for my class roster so they can send students discounted access codes. Can I share it?
reference: Not without checking FERPA constraints first — and in most cases, no. A class roster linking named students to enrollment in a specific course is generally non-directory education-record information under FERPA, which Duke cannot disclose to an outside commercial party without student consent. Even elements Duke may treat as directory information (per the Registrar's FERPA guidance, registrar.duke.edu) can't be released for students who have requested a FERPA block, and Duke policy restricts releasing student lists for commercial solicitation regardless. The compliant alternatives: have the publisher provide a generic sign-up link or access codes you distribute yourself via Canvas or class email, so students opt in without their enrollment data leaving Duke. If the publisher needs roster integration (e.g., for courseware), route it through official channels — the bookstore or OIT — where a contract and data agreement can cover it. When in doubt, ask the Office of the University Registrar before releasing anything.

question: Can I have Duke GPT grade my students' short-answer quizzes and enter those scores directly as their grades?
reference: No — not as an autonomous grader. Duke's guidance on AI use in teaching treats AI tools as assistive: the instructor of record remains responsible for evaluation of student work, so AI-produced scores cannot become grades without meaningful human review of each determination. Two additional policy considerations: (1) Data — Duke GPT (via Duke's AI Gateway) is the right venue for student work compared to consumer tools, since it operates under Duke's agreements, but you should still limit identifying details where possible. (2) Transparency — your syllabus should disclose how AI is used in assessment, consistent with your school's academic policies; students assessed by an undisclosed automated process is the scenario academic-integrity offices flag. A compliant workflow: use Duke GPT to produce draft scores or rubric-based feedback suggestions, then review and confirm each grade yourself before entry. For questions on AI tool data permissions, contact the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200; for assessment policy, consult your school's teaching guidance.

question: I recorded my seminar over Zoom and students are visible on camera asking questions. Can I post the recording publicly on YouTube as course marketing?
reference: No, not without each visible student's consent. A class recording in which students are identifiable (image, voice, name on screen) is an education record under FERPA, so public posting requires written consent from every identifiable student — enrollment-wide assumptions or syllabus boilerplate don't substitute for it. Compliant options: (1) keep the recording inside Duke-managed course platforms (Canvas with Duke's media tools such as Warpwire/Panopto), where access is limited to the class; (2) edit the recording to remove or blur student appearances — a version showing only you presenting can be shared more freely; (3) for marketing, record a standalone session without students. Also check your school's classroom recording policy, which typically requires notifying students that sessions are recorded at all. For FERPA questions, consult the Registrar's FERPA guidance (registrar.duke.edu); for media tool help, contact the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200.

question: I'm a faculty member leaving Duke for another university. Can I take my research data with me?
reference: It depends — and the default is that you must arrange it, not just copy it. Under Duke's research data policy, research data generated at Duke is generally owned or stewarded by the university (a condition of sponsored funding), even though you lead the research. What usually happens: you request a data transfer, and Duke's research administration (Office of Research & Innovation, with your school's research office) reviews sponsor terms, IRB constraints, export controls, and collaborator rights, then documents the transfer — often via a Data Transfer Agreement with your new institution. Human-subjects data adds IRB conditions: your protocol and participant consents must permit the data moving with you, and protocols typically transfer or close out formally. What you must NOT do is bulk-copy datasets to personal storage on your way out — that can breach sponsor agreements and Duke policy even when the science is yours. Start the conversation with your department research administrator well before your departure date.

question: Our department found a great web-based scheduling tool. Can I sign us up with my Duke email and start uploading our staff directory and schedules?
reference: Not before the tool goes through Duke's review channels. Buying or adopting software that will hold Duke institutional data — even 'just' a staff directory with names, emails, and schedules (Internal/Sensitive under the Data Classification Policy) — requires the IT procurement path: a security review by the IT Security Office (so Duke can vet the vendor's data handling) and, where data is involved, contract terms or a data protection agreement Duke negotiates centrally. Individual sign-ups with a Duke email don't create any of those protections, and self-purchased SaaS is exactly the 'shadow IT' case the acceptable-use and procurement policies are written to prevent. The right path: check whether OIT already licenses an equivalent tool (many scheduling needs are covered by Duke's existing Microsoft/Google tooling), and if not, submit the tool through your department's procurement process so it gets the vendor security review. Your local IT support group or the OIT Service Desk (919-684-2200) can route the request.
